key_stats: Summer 1867: Crisis in Abyssinia brewing for four years
19 August 1867: British cabinet meeting at 10 Downing Street with Lord Derby
January 1868: 13,000 soldiers landed with 20 miles of railway track and 44 elephants
44 elephants: Seven more than Hannibal took to Italy
20,000 Austrian Maria Theresa silver talas produced per week by Vienna mint
10 million pounds: Final cost to British taxpayer (initial budget 2 million, balloons to 4 million)
1741: First minting of Austrian silver tala by Maria Theresa
1780 edition: Most valued version of the Maria Theresa coin in East Africa
1950s: Maria Theresa coins still used as currency in East Africa
25 January 1868: Napier ready to set off for trek to Magdala with 5,000 men spearhead and 7,000 supply line guards
350 miles: Distance through gorges and ravines to Magdala after reaching 8,000 feet plateau
December 1867: Travelers arrived at Magdala with news that British had landed on coast

pending_qa.q: What technological innovations did Napier incorporate into the Abyssinian expedition to maintain control and logistics?
pending_qa.r: Napier brought seven photographers, a portable telegraph system, water pumps, flares to light up camp at night, and copper telegraph wire. His sappers unspooled copper wire all the way to their advance guard as they progressed. The campaign was described as the most technologically advanced military campaign in history, including 20 miles of railway track, pile driving machinery, and hundreds of tons of coal.

pending_qa.q: Why was the Austrian Maria Theresa silver coin still used as currency in East Africa in the 1950s?
pending_qa.r: The reason why these coins became entrenched and accepted in East Africa remains undetermined. The coins had simply become so accepted as a standard that they persisted as currency long after their original circulation period, remaining in use in the 1950s despite no longer being minted in Vienna.

pending_qa.q: What were the challenges facing British military planners in launching an intervention against Emperor Teodros in Abyssinia?
pending_qa.r: Intelligence was absolutely useless with the Abyssinian interior not properly mapped and consisting of challenging mountains. British officers in Bombay concluded that 'there are few countries about which we know less.' They did not know where Teodros was located, how much local support he had, which way local warlords would respond, where to land, what route to take to Magdala, or how to extract their forces without being attacked.
